stories.summary: Amit says he was always an atheist, but as an 'immature' teen he briefly held a vague belief that spirituality is different from religion and that some vast, unknowable presence governs us all. Life and rationality soon cured him of it. He grants that many people turn to atheism as a rebellion against convention, and that this may have been part of his story too. He only began thinking about atheism seriously as an adult, and his definition of it took shape over a long time.
stories.insight: Disbelief can be something you reason your way into slowly rather than a single act of rebellion. The 'spiritual but not religious' stage is often a halfway house.
stories.quote: But I was soon disabused of that notion by life and rationality.

stories.topic: The Stamp-Collector's Letter to The Economist
stories.summary: Around 2007, when Amit wrote his first columns on atheism, The Economist had described atheism as a kind of new religion. Chad English of Ottawa wrote in to object, and Amit reads the letter in full on the show. The letter argues that atheism is a religion only in the sense that not collecting stamps is a hobby, which is why atheists don't congregate or seek power as a group. What atheists want is for officials to keep their religion out of governing, just as a 'philatelist government' that favoured stamp collectors would be a bad government. It signs off: 'See you at the next non-meeting.'
stories.insight: Atheists are not a rival tribe chasing influence. They are simply people who don't do a particular thing, and what they ask of the state is neutrality.
stories.quote: So whenever someone talks of atheism as oh you are like another religion or it's a belief system, I say that no. You know, atheism is no more a religion than not collecting stamps is a hobby.

stories.topic: Grief Without God: Writing After His Mother's Death
stories.summary: Amit's mother died in 2007. In 2008 he wrote a column for Mail Today called 'What's Consolation for an Atheist?' that took on the one function of religion he admits he cannot replace: comfort in the face of death. He concluded that he couldn't start believing a fiction just to console himself. Grief is grief and has to be dealt with. He adds that he doubts religion consoles much either.
stories.insight: Intellectual honesty sometimes costs you comfort. Amit openly gives up this one piece of ground to religion rather than pretend that reason solves everything.
stories.quote: I can't help being an atheist. I'm not going to start believing in a fiction because I need to console myself.

stories.summary: In 2005 the Kansas School Board was trying to teach creationism. Bobby Henderson wrote to them demanding equal treatment for his own faith, Pastafarianism, whose god is the Flying Spaghetti Monster, and insisting that his beliefs must not be offended either. Around 2007 Amit borrowed the idea for a free-speech column called 'Don't Insult Pasta', declaring himself a proud Pastafarian and demanding that nobody offend his god.
stories.insight: Gentle satire can expose how arbitrary demands for religious privilege and 'hurt sentiments' are, without any hostility. Amit says he prefers this benign way of protesting religion.
stories.quote: You know, if you don't want me to offend your God, don't offend mine. Say nothing about pasta.

stories.topic: Ashok Desai on Why Some God-Stories Survive
stories.summary: Ajay passes on an insight from Ashok Desai. Oral traditions were a competition in which people invented and mutated countless stories, and only the ones that were cute and clicked with the human mind got remembered. So the human mind came first, and the sun god and wind god were the hits that survived. Ajay compares it to the many subreddits about JFK's murder, of which only a few become prominent.
stories.insight: Myths spread by something like natural selection among stories. What survives is whatever fits human cognition best, which need not be what is true.
stories.quote: So sort of like there are fifty thousand subreddits about the murder of JFK, and a couple of them gain prominence because they just fit in the human mind better.

stories.topic: His Father's Exit From Hinduism and a Family That Never Went Back
stories.summary: Ajay's father grew up deeply committed to Hinduism and knew it well, then became an atheist as an adult. His atheism was relaxed: he fit in easily among religious people, as Ajay does today. After that switch, religion simply vanished from the family. Ajay and his sisters have none, and neither do their children.
stories.insight: This is a personal example of Ajay's larger thesis: religious belief that isn't instilled in childhood rarely returns, so leaving religion is a one-way door for families.
stories.quote: So it's like my father switched out of deep commitment to Hinduism and deep knowledge of Hinduism as a young person into atheism as an adult. And then it's over. My sisters and I have zero. Their kids have zero.

recommendations.creator: Robert Wright
recommendations.context: Amit's answer to the claim that morality needs religion, made while explaining how our moral instincts are hardwired.
recommendations.reason: Of the many books on natural selection, this is the one Amit picks because it deals specifically with morality. He read it 20 to 25 years ago and it stayed with him. It shows how evolution produced our better instincts, and it taught him the term 'reciprocal altruism'.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Amit mentions he cited it in a recent Seen and the Unseen episode on altruism, where he felt his guest misunderstood it.
recommendations.reason: He uses it to correct a common misreading. 'Selfish gene' does not mean humans are hardwired to be selfish. Love, care and altruism are what selfish genes produce.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Introduced as 'the great book' by Dawkins, one of the Four Horsemen of New Atheism.
recommendations.reason: Amit thinks the New Atheists make many great points about organised religion and dogma that deserve to be taken seriously, even though his own atheism is gentler.

recommendations.creator: Sam Harris
recommendations.context: Named as Sam Harris's contribution to New Atheism.
recommendations.reason: One of the founding New Atheist books whose critiques of organised religion Amit says you have to take seriously.

recommendations.creator: Sam Harris
recommendations.context: Mentioned while noting that the New Atheist movement has run its course.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great conversation podcast and says he learned a lot about the craft of podcasting from it, though Harris has since moved in different directions.

recommendations.creator: Christopher Hitchens
recommendations.context: Hitchens is named as one of the Four Horsemen of New Atheism.
recommendations.reason: Amit says he adored Hitchens and misses him. He calls his writing amazing and incredible. He admires how Hitchens, once a communist, turned away from 'that religion' and became a fearless voice against all kinds of conventional thinking.

recommendations.item: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
recommendations.creator: Hannah Arendt
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Arendt's phrase 'the banality of evil' after Ajay mentions Auschwitz.
recommendations.reason: It is a warning that ordinary people can commit extraordinary cruelty, and that neither religion nor rationality protects against it.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 Mail Today column, written after his mother died in 2007.
recommendations.reason: It is where he takes on the one function of religion he can't replace, consolation in grief, and decides he won't adopt a comforting fiction.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2007 free-speech column, inspired by Pastafarianism.
recommendations.reason: It is a playful satire on demands not to offend religious sentiment: if you don't want me to offend your god, don't offend mine.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as one of Amit's earlier pieces on atheism (2014); not discussed on air.
recommendations.reason: Further reading from Amit's own writing on atheism over the years.

recommendations.creator: Bobby Henderson
recommendations.context: Bobby Henderson's 2005 letter to the Kansas School Board, which was trying to teach creationism.
recommendations.reason: Amit's favourite example of the benign, tongue-in-cheek way to protest religion, by showing how absurd it is to demand special treatment for beliefs.

recommendations.creator: Karl Popper
recommendations.context: Ajay brings up Popper while discussing agnosticism and how strongly to hold our claims.
recommendations.reason: He finds it a lovely organising principle. A theory deserves consideration when it makes predictions that could be proven wrong, and that helps us sort our beliefs by how much confidence they deserve.

recommendations.creator: Plato
recommendations.context: Amit's first example of reasoning about morality without religion.
recommendations.reason: It shows that even if God exists, morality cannot simply come from divine command.

recommendations.creator: Immanuel Kant
recommendations.context: Amit's second example of morality derived from pure reason.
recommendations.reason: He finds the formulation 'treat people as ends in themselves, not as means to an end' incredibly deep and beautiful. He says it enriches how we engage with others and has nothing to do with religion.

recommendations.creator: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
recommendations.context: Amit's third secular moral framework: the greatest good for the greatest number.
recommendations.reason: He thinks it is sound on the whole and worth knowing, but critiques it with Hayek's knowledge problem: the world is too complex to know the consequences of our actions.

recommendations.creator: Aristotle
recommendations.reason: It appeals to him because it identifies ways of behaving that make everybody better off and lead to human prosperity, without needing religion.

core_ideas.concept: Atheism Is an Absence of Belief, Not a Belief
core_ideas.explanation: The '-ism' misleads people into treating atheism as a belief system. 'I believe there is no God' claims a certainty nobody can have, because you can't prove a negative. 'I don't believe there is a God' just withholds belief from something unproven, the same way you'd withhold belief in pink fairies. The burden of proof lies with whoever asserts the claim. A rationalist atheist would become a believer if God's existence were ever actually proven.
core_ideas.quote: The correct definition involves not belief but an absence of belief.

core_ideas.concept: Atheist and Agnostic Are Different Axes, Not Points on One Line
core_ideas.explanation: People picture a line running believer, agnostic, atheist, with the agnostic as the undecided middle. In fact the two words answer different questions. Atheism is about belief. Agnosticism, from 'gnosis', is about knowledge: the view that the truth about God cannot be known. So you can be a believer and an agnostic, or, like Amit, an atheist and an agnostic.
core_ideas.quote: Atheism is about belief. Agnostic is about knowledge.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay builds on Popper's falsifiability to sort beliefs into four bins. The first is fanciful nonsense that will never produce a testable claim, like Chariots of the Gods. The second is beliefs held because of social programming, peer pressure or political convenience, which everyone has and should be aware of. The third is working bets you expect future evidence to settle. The fourth is hard knowledge built on falsifiable propositions that have held up, like evolutionary biology. Knowing which bin a belief sits in tells you how strongly to hold it.
core_ideas.quote: So, gentle reader, if you're embarrassed to believe some things that you're not yet ready to prove, great. Welcome aboard.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Jobs Religion Does, and Which Ones Reason Can Take Over
core_ideas.explanation: Amit lists four functions religion has served: explanation, meaning, morality and consolation. Science has largely replaced explanation. Meaning has to come from reality rather than invented stories. Morality can be derived without God. Consolation in the face of death is the one function he concedes he has no convincing answer for.
core_ideas.quote: I think that we have to find meaning if meaning is to be found out of reality and not out of manufactured fiction, because then that meaning would also make no sense. It would be fake and shallow.

core_ideas.explanation: Early humans filled whatever they couldn't explain with gods: a sun god, a wind god. As knowledge filled the gaps, these gods gradually disappeared. Some questions may never be answered, but an unanswered question is not evidence for God.
core_ideas.quote: And there are certain questions we simply cannot answer, but that doesn't mean that God is the answer.

core_ideas.concept: Morality Comes First, Religion Writes It Down Later
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's sequence starts with evolution, which hardwires moral instincts like compassion and caring for kin. Living together then produces norms such as not stealing, not killing, and treating others as you'd want to be treated. These norms vary with local conditions: polygamy where war has left too few men, a ban on pork where pigs spread disease. Religion arrives last, codifies those norms, and sometimes hardens them into dogma. Reason sits on top and lets humans correct their own hardwiring.
core_ideas.quote: So I would actually say that religion came later. First we have the hardwiring, then people live together, then you have the norms, then religion kind of codifies it.

core_ideas.concept: Reciprocal Altruism: The Selfish Gene Makes Us Loving
core_ideas.explanation: Feelings like compassion and family love are genuine, not hypocrisy. They evolved because they helped our genes spread, so the ultimate cause differs from the felt, proximate one. The common misreading is that a selfish gene makes us selfish. In fact it wires us to care, especially for kin. Favouring kin is the bias that reason later has to correct.
core_ideas.quote: We're hardwired to love, we are hardwired to care.

core_ideas.explanation: Plato asks whether something is good because God wills it, or whether God wills it because it is good. If the first, morality is arbitrary and we have no agency. If the second, goodness exists independently of God and before God, so God is merely a broker passing it on. Either way, morality does not depend on religion.
core_ideas.quote: God could go mad one day and will any damn thing and we have to do it. And that just doesn't make sense.

core_ideas.explanation: Several philosophical traditions reach morality without God. Kant's categorical imperative says to treat people as ends, never merely as means. Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism seeks the greatest good for the greatest number, though Amit's critique is Hayek's knowledge problem: we can't know the consequences of our actions. Aristotle's virtue ethics looks for the dispositions that lead to human flourishing. These schools disagree with each other, and that is fine.
core_ideas.quote: All these schools of thought illustrate that we are arriving at different ways of thinking about morality and thinking about the world independent of religion.

core_ideas.concept: The Religion Gene as a Military Advantage
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay sets out the standard evolutionary story. Hunter-gatherer bands averaged about 150 people. Mutations that enabled religious behaviour let much larger groups cooperate as fanatics for an invisible cause. The resulting bigger armies beat smaller secular ones, so the trait spread. There may even be a 'God gene' because believing helped us survive.
core_ideas.quote: So that's a nice simple logic that if we are able to be fanatics and believe some fanciful story, it actually improves our odds of survival directly.

core_ideas.concept: New Atheism: Every Believer Is Already an Atheist
core_ideas.explanation: About two decades ago, the 'Four Horsemen' (Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris, Daniel Dennett and Christopher Hitchens) launched a more assertive atheism. They argued that religion causes real harm through irrationality and dogma, and must be spoken against. Ironically, their assertiveness made atheism look like just another competing 'ism'. Amit thinks the movement has played itself out. Ajay counters that the rise of right-wing religious nationalism may justify calling out harmful old beliefs more firmly today.
core_ideas.quote: Dawkins beautifully pointed out that actually every believer is an atheist because you believe in your one religion. But you are an atheist for all the other bloody religions, right?

core_ideas.concept: Why Religiosity's Decline Is a One-Way Door
core_ideas.explanation: Surveys show religiosity falling worldwide. It fell first in post-war Western Europe, where after Auschwitz faith in a benign, all-powerful God became hard to sustain. It held up in the US for a while, then collapsed there too over the last 25 years. Ajay offers two mechanisms. First, faith that isn't instilled in childhood seems as strange as another religion's beliefs, so families that leave never return, and the process only runs one way. Second, conformity: when 70 to 80 percent are religious, people go along, but once belief falls below a critical mass people say openly that they don't care, and the decline accelerates.
core_ideas.quote: So it's like once it's gone, it can never come back.

core_ideas.concept: The Banality of Evil, and Prosperity as the Best Safeguard
core_ideas.explanation: Following Hannah Arendt, Amit warns that ordinary people can suddenly commit terrible cruelty, and that neither religion nor rationality prevents it. His tentative answer is prosperity, because people with good lives have an incentive to keep the peace, while scarcity and turmoil wear morality down. Ajay pushes back with Nazi Germany, 'the land of Albert Einstein and Beethoven'. Amit replies that Hitler rose out of the ruin and torment that followed World War One.
core_ideas.quote: perhaps the best answer to get to the kind of morality we would all like is a rising GDP.

core_ideas.explanation: Organised religion is declining, but the urge to adopt a belief system remains. It reappears in ideologies such as Marxism and, today, wokeism, each with its own dogma and excommunications. Amit compares how cancellation spreads (defend someone who has been cast out and you are cast out too) to Pakistan's blasphemy law. His test for whether someone is thinking independently: do they accept an ideological tribe's whole package?
core_ideas.quote: So whenever anyone conforms to the entire belief package of some ideological tribe, I know they're not thinking independently for themselves.

core_ideas.concept: Keep the Tradition, Drop the Dogma
core_ideas.explanation: Don't throw the baby out with the bathwater. Festivals and rituals give comfort and community, and they evolved for a reason. Refusing to celebrate Diwali because you don't believe in Hinduism makes no sense when family gathers and there is light everywhere. Reject the regressive, misogynistic customs and embrace the life-affirming ones, without ever coercing anyone.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need to believe in God to, you know, celebrate a tradition like that.

core_ideas.concept: The Greatest Religion: Treat People as Ends
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's final exhortation is that whether you are religious or an atheist, you should not impose your beliefs on others. Atheists who mock believers are behaving badly too. Many of Amit's friends are religious, and neither side tries to dictate to the other.
core_ideas.quote: I think the greatest religion is to treat other human beings as actual people and not as means to an end.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit isn't impressed by talk of a future woman US president, since Hillary Clinton already won the popular vote in 2016. His real benchmark: 'what I would love to see is, say, a gay atheist in the White House. You know, that'll be the day when I'll say society has really progressed.'
Chad English's letter to The Economist, read by Amit: 'Atheism is a religion in the same way that not collecting stamps is a hobby... See you at the next non-meeting.'

Mid-Pastafarianism, Amit swerves into diet advice: 'pasta is carbs. Gentle readers, please have a lot of meat, some fat, not much carb, pasta is evil... But except once in a while. But I'm not gonna be dogmatic about this because hey, atheists are not dogmatic, good ones.'

Ajay on Kant: 'hear no evil, see no evil, do no evil, and you will never write a bestseller... never use another human being as an instrument and you probably won't gain a lot of power.' Amit: 'Shame shame, how can you say such a thing?'

Humanists International finds that atheism or public apostasy can be punished by death in 13 countries, and that most of the UN's 193 member states persecute atheism in some form, for instance through blasphemy laws.

Richard Dawkins on the God of the Old Testament, read out by Amit: 'arguably the most unpleasant character in all fiction... a vindictive, bloodthirsty ethnic cleanser; a misogynistic, homophobic, racist, infanticidal, genocidal, filicidal, pestilential, megalomaniacal, sadomasochistic, capriciously malevolent bully.'
Douglas Adams on natural selection, quoted by Amit: 'I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.'

Austin Cline, quoted by Amit: a person who truly enjoys their life will do so regardless of whether any afterlife exists, and 'won't depend upon the existence of such a heaven in order for their lives to have meaning or purpose.'
Ajay invokes 'the famous quote' 'After Auschwitz, there can be no art' to explain why, after the war, Western Europeans found it hard to believe in a benign, all-powerful God.

Ajay's childhood read, Erich von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods, which he calls 'obscure nonsense': a fanciful story of beings from outer space starting life on Earth that 'just doesn't make a single testable proposition'.

Amit compares wokeism's cancellations to Pakistan's blasphemy law, under which defending the accused makes you a blasphemer too: 'And turtles all the way down.' He cites what happened to J.K. Rowling.
Amit sets the scene for why religion arose by describing the pre-scientific world as 'nature red in tooth and claw', where 'life is nasty, brutish, and short'.
